tier_reason: fbench.html lists Chapel 1.16.0 -fast at 0.528 and the 64-thread run at 0.0314 against C = 1, and src/chapel/README gives the raw runs (Chapel serial 0.9427 us/iteration with one runtime thread vs C 1.7858 us/iteration, ratio 0.5279, five runs each on the same laptop); code (src/chapel/fbench.chpl, src/c/fbench.c) and flags (src/chapel/Makefile --fast, src/c/Makefile -O3) are public, but the CPU is never named and the two builds use different flags, so C.

corrections.baseline: C fbench (src/c/fbench.c, glibc libm trig functions) built with GCC 5.4.0 'gcc -Wall -O3 -lm' (src/c/Makefile, no -march), 166,051,660 iterations, mean 296.536 s, 1.7858 us per iteration on the same Dell laptop under Xubuntu. The fbench.html table labels the C row 'GCC 3.2.3 -O3', but the 2017 Chapel and JavaScript notes (src/chapel/README, src/javascript/README) both use this GCC 5.4.0 run.
corrections.claimed_speedup: fbench.html relative time (C = 1): Chapel 1.16.0 --fast 0.528 (about 1.9x faster than C, derived from page data). src/chapel/README: serial build with CHPL_RT_NUM_THREADS_PER_LOCALE=1, 250,000,000 iterations, mean 235.68 s = 0.9427 us/iteration vs C 1.7858 us/iteration, ratio 0.5279; with the default runtime (two threads even in the serial build) user time was 1.1982 us/iteration. The 0.0314 row is a pariter=64 build on the 64-core server Pallas (14.00 s real for 250,000,000 iterations), parallel Chapel against serial C, not comparable.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Chapel 1.16.0 'chpl --fast' (= --no-checks, -O, --specialize); with the GNU backend Chapel 1.16 compiles the generated C at -O3 and, by its defaults (util/chplenv/chpl_arch.py sets CHPL_TARGET_ARCH=native on Linux with CHPL_COMM=none; make/compiler/Makefile.gnu SPECIALIZE_CFLAGS), with -march=native; backend GCC version and the author's CHPL_* settings not stated. C baseline: GCC 5.4.0 'gcc -Wall -O3 -lm' without -march.
corrections.hardware: Dell laptop running Xubuntu Linux with eight cores (CPU model not stated); the parallel rows ran on the 64-core Fourmilab server Pallas (CPU not stated).
corrections.caveats: Single-author runs on an unnamed CPU. The C row on fbench.html says GCC 3.2.3, but the Chapel comparison used a GCC 5.4.0 -O3 C run (shared with the JavaScript notes), so the old-compiler confound in the search record is wrong; the real confounds are that the builds are not flag-equivalent (Chapel's --fast adds -march=native by default, the C Makefile has none) and that both sides call the same glibc libm trig functions, whose speed the author himself suspected (src/javascript/README: a recent GCC math library slowed trig 'perhaps by as much as a factor of two'; a glibc 2.23 AVX-SSE transition regression in sin/cos, Ubuntu Launchpad 1663280, is a candidate, search snippet only). The Chapel loop discards each iteration's result except the last (C stores into globals), which lets the backend drop pure arithmetic but not the errno-setting libm calls; not checked in generated code. A latent port bug (flat-surface marginal branch computes -(asin(n1/n2))*sin(a) instead of -asin((n1/n2)*sin(a))) is dead code for the all-curved Wyld lens. The 0.0314 row compares 64-thread Chapel with serial C. Chapel 1.16.0 dates from 2017. License is CC BY-SA 4.0 (LICENSE.md), not an OSI software license.
corrections.why_faster: Not established by the sources. chpl --fast compiles the generated C with GCC -O3 plus -march=native by Chapel 1.16 defaults, while the C baseline is -O3 without -march; both call the same glibc libm sin/cos/tan/asin. The author's own notes blame slow GCC-era libm trig, so the 1.9x is a build or platform effect on the C side, not demonstrated Chapel codegen.

notes: Numbers on fbench.html and src/chapel/README match the record; tier stays C. Shortcomings: baseline is GCC 5.4.0 -O3 (not 3.2.3) on an unnamed CPU, Chapel build adds -march=native, same libm underneath, mechanism unexplained, parallel row not comparable, license CC BY-SA 4.0 (corrected from null).

tier_reason: First-party README: BenchmarkTools timings (104x104 Float64, 150x150 Complex) and log-log plots (assets/F64_mul.png, F32_mul.png, C64_mul.png) against OpenBLAS with 6 threads, with Julia 1.4.0-rc2.0 and the Ryzen 5 2600 named; no benchmark script in the repo and the OpenBLAS version is unstated, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 104x104 Float64 mul!: LinearAlgebra/OpenBLAS 68.529 us vs Gaius 31.220 us (about 2.2x faster, derived from page data); A*B 68.949 us vs Gaius.mul 32.950 us (about 2.1x, derived); 150x150 Complex{Float64}: Gaius on StructArrays 515.587 us vs OpenBLAS 546.481 us (about 1.06x, derived). Plots: 'Gaius outperforms OpenBLAS over a large range of matrix sizes, but does begin to appreciably fall behind around 800 x 800 matrices for Float64 and 650 x 650 matrices for Float32'; the plots also show OpenBLAS ahead at the smallest size (about 2x2). Integer plots compare with Julia's generic matmul, not C.
corrections.caveats: Author-run on Julia 1.4.0-rc2.0 (2020, LLVM 8.0.1, Ryzen 5 2600 Zen+, no AVX-512); the repo has no benchmark script, the OpenBLAS version is unstated, and the BLAS thread count for the REPL timings is not shown (the plots used BLAS.set_num_threads(6)). The lead is a small-to-medium size win (plots: OpenBLAS ahead at about 2x2 and beyond about 800 for Float64, 650 for Float32; Float32 is roughly level near 60-100), plausibly helped by OpenBLAS's threading overhead at small sizes (not measured). Different algorithm (recursive divide-and-conquer vs OpenBLAS's packed GEMM). Integer results compare with Julia's single-threaded generic matmul, not with C. The README calls Gaius unstable and unmaintained and points to Octavian.jl (already listed in wave 8) as the more performant pure-Julia BLAS; built on LoopVectorization.jl (also listed in wave 8).

notes: Record accurate apart from the claim that no numbers are printed: the README has REPL timings (68.529 vs 31.220 us at 104x104 Float64), now in claimed_speedup. Metadata checked (MIT, 119 stars, last commit 2023-05-05, abandoned). Not a wrapper of OpenBLAS, so not a duplicate; related wave-8 entries are Octavian.jl and LoopVectorization.jl.

tier_reason: The page numbers are real, but neither winning row is a valid same-work measurement: Firefox 55's SpiderMonkey memoises Math.sin/cos/tan/asin in a 4096-entry MathCache (FIREFOX_55_0_2_RELEASE js/src/jsmath.h, jsmath.cpp, jit/MCallOptimize.cpp inlineMathFunction, jit/CodeGenerator.cpp visitMathFunctionD) and fbench feeds identical arguments every iteration, so the trig work C does is skipped; Safari's 0.4237 is a cross-machine estimate (2008 Mac Pro run scaled by a Perl speed ratio). The V8 rows (1.33-1.50) are slower than C. No valid measurement of a JavaScript win remains, so D under the cross-run precedent.

corrections.baseline: C fbench (src/c/fbench.c, glibc libm trig functions) built with GCC 5.4.0 'gcc -Wall -O3 -lm' (src/c/Makefile, no -march), 166,051,660 iterations, mean 296.536 s, 1.7858 us per iteration on a Dell laptop under Xubuntu (src/javascript/README says the comparisons were made against GCC 5.4.0; the fbench.html table labels the C row 'GCC 3.2.3 -O3').
corrections.claimed_speedup: fbench.html relative time (C = 1): Firefox 55.0.2 0.372, Safari 11.0 0.424, Brave 0.18.36 1.334, Chrome 61 1.378, Chromium 60 1.386, Node.js v6.11.3 1.495. src/javascript/README: Firefox 457,577,013 iterations, five runs averaging 303.863 s (the README prints 'mean of 393.863', a typo; derived from the listed runs) = 0.6641 us/iteration, ratio 0.3719 (about 2.7x faster than C, derived from page data); Safari measured 1.6865 us/iteration on a 2008 Mac Pro and multiplied by a Perl-derived speed ratio of 0.4487 to an estimated 0.7567 us/iteration, ratio 0.4237 (estimate, not a same-machine run); the four V8 engines are 1.33-1.50x slower than C.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C: GCC 5.4.0, 'gcc -Wall -O3 -lm' without -march, glibc libm. JavaScript: Firefox 55.0.2 (SpiderMonkey; the README wrongly calls it Rhino), Safari 11.0 (11604.1.38.1.7, JavaScriptCore) on macOS, Brave 0.18.36, Chrome 61.0.3163.91, Chromium 60.0.3112.113 and Node.js v6.11.3 (all V8), default engine settings, src/javascript/fbench.js unchanged from 2005 apart from strict-mode declarations.
corrections.hardware: Dell laptop running Xubuntu Linux (CPU model not stated) for C, Firefox and the V8 engines; Safari ran on a 2008 Mac Pro (CPU not stated) and was rescaled with a Perl-measured speed ratio of 0.4487.
corrections.caveats: Firefox row: SpiderMonkey 55 routes Ion-inlined Math.sin, cos, tan and asin through MathCache (4096 entries keyed on the input double; the uncached path calls the same system libm sin as C), and every fbench iteration traces the same rays with the same arguments, so after the first iteration the trig calls are cache hits; the benchmark is, by the author's own description, dominated by trig library speed, so the 2.7x measures memoisation, not JavaScript codegen (close to the wazero and MQF cache precedents; kept as D, not rejected, because the result is correct and the C side is a real run). Safari row: cross-machine estimate from a 2008 Mac Pro scaled by a Perl run, and macOS libm differs from glibc; JavaScriptCore removed its own transcendental cache in 2013 (WebKit bug 123574, search snippet only). V8 rows (Brave, Chrome, Chromium, Node) are slower than C. The author attributes the gap to a slow GCC-era libm ('perhaps by as much as a factor of two'); a glibc 2.23 AVX-SSE transition regression in sin/cos (Ubuntu Launchpad 1663280) is a candidate, search snippet only. The fbench.html C label (GCC 3.2.3) contradicts the README's GCC 5.4.0 run. CPU not named. License is CC BY-SA 4.0 (LICENSE.md), not an OSI software license.
corrections.why_faster: Not the language. Firefox: SpiderMonkey's MathCache memoises transcendental results and fbench repeats identical arguments each iteration, so most sin/cos/tan/asin calls become table lookups while C recomputes them with glibc libm. Safari: a different machine and a different libm (macOS), rescaled by a Perl ratio. V8 engines, which compute every call, are 1.33-1.50x slower than C.

notes: Downgrade C to D: Firefox lead comes from SpiderMonkey 55's MathCache memoising repeated trig arguments (verified in Firefox 55.0.2 source), Safari lead is a cross-machine estimate, V8 engines lose to C; baseline is GCC 5.4.0 -O3 not 3.2.3. The Firefox row alone would fit the wazero/MQF cache reject precedent; kept as D since the record also holds legitimate (slower) rows. License corrected to CC-BY-SA-4.0.
